text: A murder inquiry is only as good as the institution's appetite for an answer. Cairo, days before January 2011: a detective who takes his cut like everyone around him is handed the death of a woman in a five-star hotel, and the case climbs toward people he is not supposed to touch while the streets outside begin to fill. Tarik Saleh keeps the furniture of the crime film intact: the interview room, the folded bill, the file that thickens. The corrosion works underneath the genre rather than instead of it. The picture came out of Denmark and took the top dramatic prize in Sundance's world competition, an odd passport for something this exact about who in Cairo can be leaned on. Across 111 minutes the pressure sits less on the killer's identity than on how long a man is permitted to keep asking.

The 10th Battalion set a record for individual bravery awards in one battle, and a film built on that has to decide what to do with everyone who came home undecorated. Paul Gross puts a sergeant of the Fighting Tenth at the centre and then keeps leaving the front, giving a large share of his 114 minutes to a courtship and the household rooms behind it. That division is the argument. Canada's film industry named it best motion picture of its year, which fits the scale of the intention: a country's central war memory staged in full rather than referred to, with the reasoning that produced volunteers examined at home before anyone reaches the mud. The romance is not there to soften the fighting. It is the thing the fighting gets measured against.

Sosa works the corridor outside the emergency ward, and he is there for the same reason the ambulances are. He signs the injured, or their relatives, on behalf of a firm that converts insurance claims into revenue and does not treat the arrangement as something a man walks away from. Pablo Trapero shoots the trade at working speed, at night, in headlights and hallway light and paperwork pressed flat against a wall, and lets the romance with Luján, who works the same hours from the other side of the stretcher, run as part of the thriller rather than a rest from it. What holds the 107 minutes is that getting out is a practical problem before it is a moral one: a debt, an address, a signature already on file. It plays less like a case study than like a shift with no end of shift.

A note left at the wrong counter turns a bored man into the most dangerous person in the building. Miles Cullen has spent years counting other people's money at a bank branch tucked inside a Toronto shopping mall, and a few days before Christmas he comes into information he was never meant to have. Daryl Duke keeps the film in that bright public place, Christmas at full volume, where there is nowhere to stand unobserved. The pleasure across 102 minutes is procedural: a man with no criminal history reasoning his way forward one small preparation at a time, and the effort it takes to look exactly as unremarkable at his window on Tuesday as he did on Monday. Everything rests on the arithmetic of an ordinary working day, and on how well a quiet man can count.

Everything here moves by water or on foot, at the pace a canoe can be paddled and carried. Father LaForgue has crossed the ocean to bring Catholicism to the Algonquin, and the Algonquin who agree to take him upriver do so warily, with their own obligations and their own reading of the priest. Bruce Beresford lets the disagreement remain a disagreement. Two systems of duty, neither translated for anyone's comfort, collide over entirely practical questions: where to camp, whom to trust, what a word turns into when it is carried across a language by a man who needs it to mean one thing. The cinematography took an award in Australia and earns it plainly, by making cold and distance legible instead of handsome. At 101 minutes it is short for a journey film, and the compression keeps it from settling into pageant.

In 1960 a road through Patagonia runs long enough that a stranger driving it in convoy turns into a kind of acquaintance. Lucía Puenzo begins with that courtesy, a German doctor and an Argentinean family sharing a route toward the town where they mean to start again, and then keeps the film close to the daughter, who has begun to be looked at as a case. The audience is handed, early, more than the household has, and nobody is hurried toward it; that gap is where the 90 minutes get their pressure. Nothing raises its voice. What Puenzo is examining is how measurement and improvement can be offered as kindness inside a house where the parents are grateful for the attention, and how hard a courtesy is to withdraw once it has been extended.

Three hours and eleven minutes, and much of that is labour: ground worked in the cold, bread counted, weeks endured in a ship's hold. Karl and Kristina Nilsson farm poor land in nineteenth-century Sweden, and the decision to leave arrives the way such decisions actually arrive, not as revelation but as arithmetic done over and over with worsening numbers, sharpened by neighbours being pressed for what they believe. Hardship is never announced. It gathers as chores, and then as weather. Jan Troell gives the ocean crossing and the overland passage their true proportion instead of a dissolve, so that Minnesota, when the fields finally resemble what was promised, has been paid for in screen time as much as in years. The argument of the film is about duration. It could not be made at ninety minutes, and it declines every chance to try.

Ownership of the hill changes several times a day, which makes it less a position than a ledger nobody is allowed to close. By 1951 the negotiating has started and the killing has not, and the patch of ground being fought over will decide where a line falls on a map, which means the men on it are dying for a cartographer. Jang Hoon threads a second mechanism through the picture: an officer sent up not to fight but to look into something the unit has not reported, so the war is under inquiry while it is still being conducted. That gives the 133 minutes a shape most combat films lack. What accumulates is a particular exhaustion, produced by knowing the date the shooting ends but not the hour, and by taking ground that will be lost by lunch and retaken before dark.

The narrator is a fish, and it is not a joke the film makes once and drops. A young woman drives away from a collision she caused, and the picture that follows her keeps slipping its register: guilt treated as a physical condition, a stranger named Evian turning up with an offer, a voice from underwater that appears to know the entire shape of the thing. Denis Villeneuve holds the 87 minutes close to her body and its refusals, so the fable stays tethered to something that can bruise. It went out as Canada's submission to the Academy that year, a strange errand for a French-language picture narrated by a fish. It works because it never asks to be decoded. It proceeds deadpan, as though everyone had agreed in advance that the fish was a reliable witness.

Between a wounded man and a hospital abroad stand a plane ticket and the money for it. An armed veteran of the Iran-Iraq War, unable to raise that money for his comrade, takes a travel agency and everyone inside it. Ebrahim Hatamikia holds almost the whole film in that room, which turns it into an argument conducted at gunpoint about what a country owes the men it sent, and, less comfortably, what the strangers on the floor owe them. Audiences at home voted it their film of the year, an unusual verdict for a picture whose hostage-taker spends 108 minutes asking the room to agree with him. Nobody is written as a monster, and the position of the man with the weapon is never made easy to dismiss or easy to accept.

Survivors of a torpedoed British ship end up aboard the U-boat that sank them, lost in fog. That is the good half hour: one submarine, two crews, a corridor too narrow for anyone to pass without deciding something, and no reliable idea where they are. The trick is that the two crews never stop being two crews; whatever cooperation exists is temporary and openly conditional. Then the fog opens on Caprona, and there are dinosaurs. Kevin Connor plays the first part straight, which is exactly why the second part goes down; the creatures are the handmade sort, worked by people rather than processors, moving at the speed such things move, and the film shoots around the seams without apology. Ninety minutes, no slack, running on the old pulp principle that any premise is acceptable if events arrive in a sensible order.

A boy loses his grip on his father and his small sister while fleeing during the Korean War, and spends the next several decades keeping a promise made in that minute. JK Youn runs Duk-soo's life along the routes his country's poorest actually travelled, down a German coal mine and then into Vietnam, so a family melodrama doubles as a record of where the household money came from. The method is unembarrassed: 126 minutes built to produce tears on schedule, and it never pretends otherwise. The engineering is visible and it still works. What makes it worth sitting with is the arithmetic underneath. Every decade Duk-soo works, somebody at home is fed, schooled or married off, and the ledger stays visible on screen, including the question of whether the debt was fairly assigned to one man.
